Before documenting or shipping a feature as a security control, verify it actually enforces the guarantee in every realistic scenario, and be explicit about its limits. Many "safety" mechanisms look sound but have edge cases that undermine them entirely:

- Allowlists/denylists must match on exact, whole values rather than prefixes. A prefix check like `cmd.startsWith("git diff")` can be bypassed by appending arguments, and even an "obviously read-only" command (e.g. `git diff`, `git status`) can execute arbitrary code if the environment is configured to do so (e.g. `diff.external`, `core.fsmonitor`). Narrow the allowlist to exact, fully-specified commands, and document the trust assumption explicitly (e.g. "only auto-approve this in repositories you trust").
- Ignore/ exclusion patterns that protect secrets or sensitive cached data must account for all the places the data can appear. A root-anchored `.gitignore` entry (`.cline/enterprise/`) won't match the same folder nested in a subdirectory; use a recursive pattern (`**/.cline/enterprise/`) and verify with a tool like `git check-ignore` that it actually matches nested paths before relying on it to keep access keys or other secrets out of version control.
- Don't label something a "security mechanism" if it's trivially defeated by the component it's supposed to control (e.g., a hook meant to stop a model from reading a file, when the model can simply ignore or route around it). If the mechanism is a best-effort convenience filter rather than a real boundary, frame and document it that way instead of implying a security guarantee it can't deliver.

When reviewing code or docs that introduce any gatekeeping, filtering, or exclusion logic intended to protect data or restrict behavior, explicitly test the bypass cases, tighten matching logic, and ensure the stated guarantee matches what the implementation can actually enforce.</description>
